title: AI Guardrails
description: AI guardrails are deliberate controls around model calls that limit what may enter a prompt, what may leave as a reply, and which side effects require a human gate.

title: AI Observability
description: AI observability is telemetry purpose-built for models: traces across retrieval and generation, versioned prompts and model IDs, quality and safety eval signals, cost and latency per feature — not just whether CPUs are busy.

title: Feature Stores – System Design Practices
description: A feature store is a governed platform for machine-learning features: named, versioned computations over operational and analytical data that training and serving both consume from the same definition.

title: LLM Architecture – System Design Practices
description: LLM architecture is how you run transformer language models in production: tokenize prompts, run prefill and decode phases, manage the growing key-value (KV) cache, and stream tokens back to clients.

title: ML System Architecture
description: ML system architecture maps machine learning work into explicit layers—data and features, training, registry, serving, and monitoring—so models ship as versioned products with owners and SLOs, not ad hoc notebooks on a shared drive.

title: ML System Design – System Design Practices
description: Product ranking for an e-commerce catalog is a production ML system, not a single model file.

title: MLOps – System Design Practices
description: MLOps applies DevOps discipline to the full machine-learning lifecycle: versioned data and code, automated training and evaluation, staged promotion to serving, production monitoring, and retraining triggers — treating each hop as a repr…

title: Model Monitoring – System Design Practices
description: Model monitoring observes production ML beyond CPU graphs: it tracks whether inputs, outputs, and delayed labels still match what the model was trained to handle.

title: Model Serving – System Design Practices
description: Model serving at an e-commerce retailer is how the Catalog search ranking model reaches shoppers.

title: Model Training at Scale
description: A model training pipeline is a declarative, repeatable workflow that snapshots labeled data, prepares features, trains, evaluates, and registers artifacts when quality gates pass—each step caching outputs so experiments do not recompute…

title: Prompt Engineering
description: Prompt engineering is how teams turn brittle chat strings into versioned templates, typed variables, and measured behavior before production.

title: RAG Architecture – System Design Practices
description: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers questions by retrieving relevant passages from an indexed corpus and conditioning the LLM on that evidence at inference time.

title: Training Pipelines – System Design Practices
description: At a ride-hailing product, a training pipeline is the automated DAG that turns historical trip and demand signals into a versioned zone-level demand-forecast model — the same way CI/CD turns commits into deployable artifacts.

title: Vector Databases – System Design Practices
description: A vector database stores embedding vectors and answers approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) queries: given a query embedding, return the IDs whose vectors are closest in cosine or dot-product space.

title: Big Ball of Mud – System Design Practices
description: A Big Ball of Mud is a system with no enforceable structure: modules call modules in every direction, domain rules live wherever the last sprint left them, and the only way to predict behavior is to trace code by hand.

title: Chatty I/O
description: Chatty I/O is a performance anti-pattern where code issues many fine-grained reads or remote calls inside a loop instead of batching or joining up front.

title: Chatty Services
description: Chatty services exchange many fine-grained synchronous RPCs for one user action.

title: Distributed Monolith – System Design Practices
description: A distributed monolith is a microservices layout that keeps monolith coupling but adds network hops.

title: God Object / God Service – System Design Practices
description: A god object (or god class) is a type that knows too much and does too much: its public surface spans unrelated capabilities, it reaches into other modules’ data, and most features route through it.

title: God Service
description: A god service is a deployable that owns more business capabilities than one team can evolve on its own schedule.

title: Golden Hammer – System Design Practices
description: Golden Hammer is the habit of solving every new problem with a tool the team already trusts, even when the problem’s shape does not fit that tool.

title: Leaky Abstractions
description: A leaky abstraction sells a simple surface while hiding mechanics callers must still understand to stay correct.

title: Magic Pushbutton – System Design Practices
description: Magic Pushbutton is the belief that a product, platform, or vendor feature can replace disciplined workflow design.

title: Premature Optimization – System Design Practices
description: Premature optimization is spending engineering effort on speed or scale before evidence shows where time and money actually go.

title: Resume-Driven Development – System Design Practices
description: Resume-driven development (RDD) is choosing technology to pad individual credentials instead of matching system requirements.

title: Shared Database
description: The shared database anti-pattern lets multiple services read and write the same tables as if they were one application.

title: Tight Coupling
description: Tight coupling means a change in one module forces coordinated changes in others — at compile time, deploy time, or runtime.

title: Vendor Lock-in – System Design Practices
description: Vendor lock-in is dependency deep enough that leaving a supplier becomes economically or technically prohibitive.

title: API Authentication
description: API authentication is how a resource server decides which principal—human user, OAuth client, service account, or device—is calling before it runs business logic.

title: API Authorization
description: API authorization decides whether an authenticated principal may perform an action on a specific resource.

title: API Gateway
description: An API gateway is the controlled entry point for north-south API traffic.

title: API Pagination
description: API pagination splits large collections into fixed-size pages so list endpoints return bounded payloads.

title: API Rate Limiting
description: API rate limiting caps how many requests a client may send in a time window, protecting upstream capacity, enforcing commercial tiers, and slowing abuse.

title: API Versioning
description: API versioning is how you evolve an HTTP API’s contract without stranding existing clients.

title: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
description: The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern gives each major client experience its own backend service that shapes data and protocols for that UI.

title: Contract Testing
description: Contract testing checks that an API provider’s behaviour matches what its consumers rely on, without standing up every dependent service in one integration environment.

title: API Filtering and Sorting
description: API filtering and sorting are conventions for narrowing and ordering collection responses over HTTP—typically query parameters on GET /resources.

title: GraphQL
description: GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a runtime that executes those queries against a type system.

title: gRPC
description: gRPC is a high-performance remote procedure call (RPC) framework: you define a service and messages in a .proto file, run the Protocol Buffers compiler to generate typed stubs, and exchange binary Protobuf payloads over HTTP/2 (multiplex…

title: HATEOAS
description: HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) is a REST constraint: the server tells the client which transitions are available by embedding links (and sometimes action metadata) in representations, so the client starts from a…

title: OpenAPI Specification
description: The OpenAPI Specification (OAS; formerly Swagger) is a vendor-neutral, machine-readable format—YAML or JSON—for describing HTTP APIs.

title: REST API Design
description: REST API design is the practice of exposing domain resources over HTTP using a uniform interface: nouns in URIs, semantics in methods and status codes, and state carried in representations (usually JSON) rather than on the server between…

title: Clean Architecture
description: Clean Architecture organizes code as concentric rings so business rules sit at the center and every outer layer depends inward.

title: CQRS Pattern
description: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits commands that change state from queries that return data, often with separate models and stores for each side.

title: Data Mesh Architecture
description: Data Mesh is a sociotechnical approach to analytics where each business domain owns the data it produces and publishes that data as a discoverable data product with documented interfaces.

title: Event-Driven Architecture
description: In event-driven architecture (EDA), a service publishes a domain event when something meaningful happens instead of calling the next service synchronously and waiting.

title: Event Sourcing
description: In event sourcing, the system of record is an append-only log of domain events, not a row that gets overwritten in place.

title: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)
description: The domain interacts with the outside world only through well-defined interfaces called ports.

title: Microservices Architecture
description: Microservices are independently deployable services, each owning its data and exposing a narrow business capability over the network.

title: Modular Monolith
description: A modular monolith is still one deployable, but internal modules behave like miniature services: each exposes a public API, owns its data, and hides implementation details.

title: Monolith Architecture
description: A monolith is one deployable application: every module runs in the same process and typically talks to one primary database through shared connection pools.

title: Onion Architecture
description: Onion Architecture is Jeffrey Palermo’s domain-centric layering model: dependencies point inward toward the Domain Model at the center, with Domain Services, Application Services, and Infrastructure as outward rings.

title: Peer-to-Peer Systems
description: Peer-to-peer (P2P) systems treat every participant as both client and server.

title: Serverless Architecture
description: Serverless architecture runs your code on managed, event-triggered compute instead of servers you size and patch yourself.

title: Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)
description: Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) exposes coarse-grained business capabilities as network services, often integrated through an Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) that routes, transforms, and bridges protocols.

title: Space-Based Architecture
description: Space-Based Architecture (SBA) — also called tuple-space or cloud architecture — removes the central database from the synchronous request path.

title: Batch Processing
description: Batch processing is data computation that runs over a bounded input—files, table partitions, or a time window—on a schedule or on demand, then finishes.

title: BI & Reporting
description: BI and reporting architecture is how curated analytical data reaches business consumers through dashboards, scheduled reports, exports, and embedded analytics.

title: Data Governance for Analytics
description: Data governance for analytics is the operating model and tooling that make shared warehouses and lakehouses trustworthy: every dataset has an owner, sensitivity is classified, access is enforced at the engine, lineage is knowable, and qu…

title: Data Pipeline Patterns
description: Data pipeline patterns are reusable design choices for moving and refining data at scale: layered lakehouse layouts (medallion bronze, silver, gold), idempotent writes, incremental processing with checkpoints, orchestration, and quality…

title: Data Pipeline Design
description: A data pipeline is the end-to-end path that moves data from source systems through ingestion, validation, transformation, and publication to downstream consumers.

title: Data Quality
description: Data quality is the practice of measuring and enforcing whether analytical datasets meet agreed standards for accuracy, completeness, timeliness, validity, and consistency before and after they reach consumers.

title: Feature Stores
description: A feature store is the data-platform layer between lakehouse or warehouse tables and ML workloads.

title: Kappa Architecture
description: Kappa Architecture is a stream-first design for analytical and operational data products: one processing codebase reads an immutable event log, maintains serving views for live queries, and replays the same log when logic or schemas change.

title: Lakehouse Governance
description: Lakehouse governance is the set of policies, catalogs, and controls that make tabular data on object storage as discoverable, secure, and auditable as warehouse tables.

title: Lambda Architecture
description: Lambda architecture is a big-data pattern, popularized by Nathan Marz, that answers queries by combining three layers: an immutable master dataset of raw events, a batch layer that periodically recomputes complete views from that history…

title: ML Feature Engineering
description: ML feature engineering on a data platform is the work of turning curated warehouse and stream data into stable, entity-keyed signals models can train on and score with at runtime.

title: Real-Time Analytics
description: Real-time analytics (often implemented as real-time OLAP) is the practice of serving interactive aggregates and filters over fresh event data with sub-second query latency at high concurrency.

title: Apache Spark Architecture
description: Apache Spark is a distributed analytics engine that runs user programs as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of stages across a cluster.

title: Stream Processing
description: Stream processing is continuous computation over an unbounded sequence of events: each record arrives in order (per partition), operators update derived state or emit results, and the job keeps running until you stop it.

title: Active-Active Architecture
description: An active-active architecture serves production traffic from two or more regions (or sites) at the same time.

title: Active-Passive Architecture
description: Active-passive (primary/standby) routes production traffic through one active region or site while a secondary site remains on standby—scaled down, idle, or serving only health checks—until failover.

title: Auto-Scaling Patterns
description: Auto-scaling patterns are the recurring ways platforms add or remove compute—VMs, containers, or functions—in response to demand signals.

title: Auto-Scaling Deep Dive
description: Autoscaling (in the cloud operational sense) is the continuous matching of running capacity to load by automated policies that add or remove instances, pods, or service units based on metrics.

title: Cloud Cost Optimization
description: Cloud cost optimization is the technical and procedural work of reducing cloud spend without sacrificing reliability or performance.

title: Cloud Migration Patterns
description: Cloud migration patterns are repeatable ways to move workloads from on-premises, colocation, or another cloud into a target platform: how you classify each application, sequence dependencies, replicate data, cut over traffic, and optiona…

title: Cloud-Native Design Principles
description: Cloud-native design is the set of architectural practices that make applications fit elastic, shared cloud infrastructure: stateless processes, configuration and backing services kept outside the deployable artifact, immutable releases,…

title: Cloud-Native Principles
description: Cloud-native describes how teams design, build, and operate software to exploit public cloud characteristics: rapid provisioning through APIs, pay-for-use economics, geographic distribution, and shared responsibility with the provider.

title: Cloud Networking
description: Cloud networking is how workloads, users, and hybrid data centres meet inside a provider’s virtual network: segmenting tiers with subnets and policy, routing between virtual networks and regions, publishing DNS, and steering traffic thro…

title: Cloud Storage Patterns
description: Cloud storage patterns are the pairing of each dataset with the right primitive—object, block, file, or archive—and the lifecycle rules that automatically move cold data to cheaper tiers while keeping hot paths on low-latency media.

title: Container Orchestration
description: Container orchestration on cloud is the practice of running production container workloads on managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE) or comparable services (ECS, Cloud Run with Knative) where the control plane is operated by the provider and…

title: Disaster Recovery Patterns
description: Disaster recovery (DR) is the set of processes, infrastructure, and runbooks that restore applications and data after a major failure—regional cloud outage, datacenter loss, ransomware, or a bad deployment that cannot be rolled back in p…

title: FinOps
description: FinOps is a cross-functional operating model for managing variable cloud spend.

title: Kubernetes Architecture
description: Kubernetes architecture on cloud is the split between a provider-managed control plane (API server, scheduler, controllers, etcd) and a customer-operated data plane (nodes, pods, networking plugins).

title: Cloud Landing Zones
description: A cloud landing zone is a pre-configured, governed foundation in a public cloud: multi-account (or multi-subscription) structure, shared networking, identity integration, logging, and guardrails that every new workload inherits before ap…

title: Managed Services Strategy
description: Managed services strategy is how organisations decide which infrastructure capabilities to run as provider-operated offerings—RDS and Aurora, Azure SQL and Cosmos DB, Cloud SQL and AlloyDB; MSK, Event Hubs, and Pub/Sub; ElastiCache, Azur…

title: Multi-Cloud Strategy
description: A multi-cloud strategy is a deliberate choice to run production workloads on two or more public cloud providers, with documented reasons for placement, shared governance, and integration paths between them.

title: Multi-Region Architecture
description: Multi-region architecture distributes application and data components across two or more geographic regions within the same public cloud provider so that user traffic, batch work, or failover can continue when a region is impaired or whe…

title: Serverless Architecture
description: Serverless architecture is an execution and integration model where the cloud provider runs and scales compute, and teams pay for invocations, duration, and attached managed services rather than reserved instances.

title: Serverless Platforms
description: Serverless platforms are managed cloud runtimes that execute functions or containers without you operating servers.

title: Service Mesh in Cloud
description: A service mesh in cloud Kubernetes is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication — encryption, routing, retries, and telemetry — outside application code.

title: Shared Responsibility Model
description: The shared responsibility model is the contract-shaped mental map that splits security and compliance duties between a cloud provider and its customer.

title: Claim Check Pattern
description: The Claim Check pattern (EIP Store in Library, also called reference-based messaging) stores bulky message bodies in external object storage and sends only a lightweight claim check—URL, object key, or pre-signed token—through the broker.

title: Command Pattern
description: Command messaging packages an imperative request—“perform this action with this data”—as a typed message routed to exactly one logical handler.

title: Competing Consumers
description: Competing Consumers is a messaging pattern in which multiple identical consumer instances pull work from the same point-to-point channel and each message is processed by exactly one of them.

title: Correlation IDs
description: A correlation identifier is a unique token that marks one logical business operation across every hop—HTTP calls, queue messages, and batch jobs—so logs, metrics, and support tools can be filtered to a single story.

title: Event Notification
description: Event notification is an event-driven integration style in which a producer publishes a compact message meaning “something happened,” and interested consumers react without receiving a full copy of the producer’s entity state in the even…

title: Event Streaming
description: Event streaming is a communication and persistence pattern where producers append records to an ordered, partitioned log and consumers read forward at their own pace, retaining a cursor (offset) per partition.

title: Fan-Out / Fan-In
description: Fan-out / fan-in (EIP Scatter-Gather, also called broadcast–aggregate) is a pattern where a coordinator dispatches the same logical request to multiple independent workers in parallel, then merges their responses—fully or partially—befor…

title: Inbox Pattern
description: The inbox pattern (closely related to the idempotent consumer) makes message handling safe under at-least-once delivery.

title: Message Queues
description: Message queues implement the Enterprise Integration Patterns Point-to-Point Channel: producers send messages into a durable channel and the messaging system delivers each message to one consumer instance among a competing group.

title: Message Routing
description: Message routing is the set of patterns that decide which downstream channel or handler receives each message without hard-wiring every producer to every consumer address.

title: Publish/Subscribe (Pub/Sub)
description: Publish/subscribe (pub/sub) is an asynchronous messaging pattern in which publishers send messages to a named channel (often called a topic) without addressing individual receivers, and the messaging infrastructure delivers a copy to eve…

title: Request-Response
description: Request-response is a synchronous communication pattern in which a caller sends a message and blocks until the callee returns a reply or the call fails with a timeout or error.

title: Transactional Outbox Pattern
description: The transactional outbox pattern lets a service update persistent domain state and record an outbound message in one local database transaction.

title: Webhooks
description: Webhooks are provider-initiated HTTP callbacks: when an event occurs in a SaaS or platform system, the provider sends an HTTP request (usually POST with a JSON body) to a subscriber URL that the consumer registered in advance.

title: Data Cataloging
description: A data catalog is the organization’s searchable map of datasets, pipelines, dashboards, and models—linking physical locations to business meaning, ownership, sensitivity, and lineage.

title: Data Contracts
description: A data contract is a versioned agreement between whoever produces a dataset or event stream and the teams that consume it.

title: Data Lake
description: A data lake is a centralized repository that stores raw, semi-structured, and structured data in native formats at scale, usually on object storage, and interprets schema at read time rather than at ingest (schema-on-read).

title: Data Lakehouse
description: A data lakehouse is an architecture that keeps cheap object storage as the system of record while adding warehouse-like table semantics on top: ACID commits, schema evolution, snapshot history, and SQL access through engines such as Spar…

title: Data Modeling Patterns
description: Data modeling patterns name recurring ways to map domain concepts onto physical storage: how you represent trees, sparse attributes, time-ordered events, or polymorphic entities when a single normalized table is awkward.

title: Data Warehouse
description: A data warehouse is a centralized analytical datastore optimized for read-heavy reporting: large scans, joins across history, and repeatable aggregations that would contend with live transactions on an OLTP database.

title: Database Indexing
description: Database indexing maintains auxiliary access paths—B-tree nodes, inverted lists, block summaries—so the engine can find rows by key or predicate without scanning every page in the heap.

title: Database Per Service
description: Database per service is a microservices data pattern where each service has exclusive ownership of its persistence: no other service may read or write that database directly, and cross-service data needs are satisfied through the owning…

title: Event Store
description: An event store is an append-only persistence layer that records every domain event affecting an entity’s lifecycle instead of overwriting current state in place.

title: Graph Databases
description: A graph database persists data as nodes (entities), relationships (typed, directed edges), and properties on both.

title: Normalization vs Denormalization
description: Normalization is the process of structuring relational tables so each fact about an entity is stored once, related entities link through keys, and normal forms (commonly third normal form, 3NF, in OLTP) eliminate redundant columns that c…

title: OLTP vs OLAP
description: OLTP (online transactional processing) is the class of database workloads dominated by short, concurrent reads and writes—placing an order, updating inventory, or recording a payment—with row-oriented storage and ACID guarantees on indiv…

title: Polyglot Persistence
description: Polyglot persistence is the practice of using more than one database technology within a single system—relational, document, key-value, search, graph, or time-series—so each datastore matches the access pattern, consistency model, and sh…

title: Time-Series Databases
description: A time-series database (TSDB) optimizes for measurements stamped with time: values (fields) plus identifying dimensions (tags or labels).

title: Vector Databases
description: A vector database (or vector index inside another store) persists embeddings—fixed-length float vectors from ML models—and answers approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) queries: given a query vector, which stored vectors are closest under c…

title: Build vs Buy – System Design Practices
description: This decision is not binary.

description: The four primary caching strategies are cache-aside (lazy loading), where the application manages all cache interactions; write-through, where all writes go to both cache and database synchronously; write-behind (write-back), where write…

title: Cloud Provider Selection – System Design Practices
description: AWS holds the largest market share (~33% as of 2024) and has the broadest service catalog—over 200 services covering virtually every infrastructure use case.

title: CQRS vs CRUD
description: CRUD uses one model and API for reads and writes—simple and transactional.

title: Deployment Strategy Guide – System Design Practices
description: Deployment strategy is distinct from release strategy.

title: Elasticsearch vs OpenSearch
description: Elasticsearch (Elastic) and OpenSearch (forked from ES 7.10) provide distributed search and analytics.

title: Event-Driven vs Request-Response
description: Request-response couples caller and callee in time: the client waits for an answer.

title: Kafka vs RabbitMQ
description: Kafka is a distributed commit log optimized for high-throughput, durable retention, and multiple consumer groups reading at their own offsets.

title: Kubernetes vs Serverless
description: Kubernetes runs arbitrary containerized workloads with fine-grained control over networking, state, and scheduling.

title: Message Broker Selection – System Design Practices
description: Kafka is a distributed log optimized for high throughput, long-term message retention, and event replay.

title: Monolith vs Microservices – System Design Practices
description: This decision is rarely permanent, but reversing it is expensive.

title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC – System Design Practices
description: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2 to provide a strongly typed RPC framework optimized for performance and code generation.

title: SQL Database Selection – System Design Practices
description: PostgreSQL and MySQL have dominated open-source relational databases for two decades, with PostgreSQL growing rapidly as the preferred choice for new projects due to its superior feature set.

title: SQL vs NoSQL – System Design Practices
description: You are choosing how to store application data for years, not for a sprint demo.

title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication – System Design Practices
description: When services or components need to communicate, you choose between synchronous communication—where the caller blocks waiting for a response—and asynchronous communication—where the caller publishes a message or event and continues witho…

title: Blue-Green Deployment
description: Blue-green deployment keeps two production-identical environments—conventionally “blue” (live) and “green” (idle)—and moves user traffic from one to the other in a single switch once the new version is validated.

title: Canary Releases
description: A canary release routes a small fraction of production traffic to a new version while the stable version continues to serve the majority.

title: CI/CD Pipelines
description: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated path from source commit to running software: continuous integration merges changes to a shared trunk with automated build and test, and continuous delivery (or deployment) promotes the same validated arti…

title: Container Orchestration
description: Container orchestration is the automated placement, lifecycle, networking, and scaling of containerized workloads across a pool of machines.

title: Database Migrations
description: Database migrations are the controlled sequence of schema and data changes that keep a shared database compatible with continuously deploying applications.

title: Environment Management
description: Environment management is how teams define, provision, configure, and promote software through named stages—commonly development, staging, and production—so validation in earlier stages predicts behavior where users depend on the system.

title: Feature Flags
description: Feature flags (feature toggles) are runtime switches that choose which code path or capability is active for a request, user cohort, or environment—without redeploying application binaries.

title: GitOps
description: GitOps is an operational model for Kubernetes (and similar platforms) in which the desired cluster state is declared in Git, reviewed like application code, and continuously reconciled by controllers running inside the cluster.

title: Immutable Infrastructure
description: Immutable infrastructure means production instances are never patched, tuned, or configured live.

title: Infrastructure as Code
description: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the practice of defining networks, compute, data stores, IAM, and platform resources in version-controlled files so environments can be planned, reviewed, applied, and reproduced consistently.

title: Progressive Delivery
description: Progressive delivery is a delivery discipline that combines continuous deployment with deliberate, measurable exposure of change to production users.

title: Release Strategies
description: Release strategy is how a new software version reaches users: whether traffic shifts all at once, in waves, by percentage, or only after mirrored observation.

title: Rollback Strategies
description: Rollback strategies are planned ways to reverse or mitigate a bad production change—returning traffic to a known-good application version, disabling risky behavior, or stopping promotion before full exposure.

title: Rolling Deployments
description: A rolling deployment replaces running instances with a new version in small waves rather than stopping the entire fleet at once.

title: Service Mesh
description: A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service connectivity—encryption, identity, routing, resilience, and telemetry—outside application binaries.

title: Clock Synchronization
description: Clock synchronization in distributed systems is the problem of deciding what time an event happened when every machine keeps its own oscillator, NTP skews, and VMs pause for live migration.

title: Compensating Transactions
description: A compensating transaction is an application-defined operation that reverses the business effect of an already-committed local step when a later step in a distributed workflow fails.

title: Consensus Algorithms
description: Distributed consensus is the problem of getting a set of replicas to agree on a single value or on an append-only log order despite crash failures and unreliable networks.

title: Distributed Coordination
description: Distributed coordination is the infrastructure that lets many processes agree on small pieces of shared metadata—who is the leader, which nodes are alive, what configuration is current—without each application embedding its own consensus…

title: Distributed Locking
description: A distributed lock is a mutual-exclusion primitive that only one client in a cluster may hold at a time, usually implemented as a key in Redis, a sequential ephemeral znode in ZooKeeper, or a lease record in etcd.

title: Distributed Scheduling
description: Distributed scheduling is the decision process that maps pending units of work—Pods, batch tasks, queue messages, workflow activities—to workers with enough capacity and the right constraints.

title: Distributed Transactions
description: A distributed transaction is a coordinated unit of work that either commits or aborts across multiple independent resource managers—relational databases, message brokers, or other XA-capable stores—as if it were one atomic operation.

title: Gossip Protocols
description: Gossip protocols disseminate information the way rumors spread: each member periodically contacts a few random peers and merges what they hear.

title: Leader Election
description: Leader election is the process by which a distributed group picks one member as the authoritative coordinator for a period—handling writes, assigning partitions, running control loops, or holding a cluster-wide lock.

title: Quorum Reads & Writes
description: A quorum is the minimum number of replicas that must participate in a read or write before a distributed store acknowledges the operation.

title: Saga Pattern
description: A saga is a long-running business process implemented as a sequence of local transactions, each confined to one service and database.

title: Service Discovery
description: Service discovery maintains a live directory from service name (and optional metadata) to network locations of healthy instances.

title: Split Brain Problem
description: Split brain is a failure mode in replicated systems where two or more nodes each believe they are the authoritative primary and accept conflicting writes during or after a network partition.

title: Vector Clocks
description: A vector clock is an array (or map) of counters—one component per participating node—where component i counts events known from node i.

title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
description: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short, durable note that captures why the team made a significant design choice.

title: Architecture Principles
description: Architecture principles are short, durable rules of thumb that steer design when requirements conflict.

title: Backward Compatibility
description: Backward compatibility means a new version of a producer still satisfies existing consumers built against an older contract.

title: Bounded Contexts
description: A bounded context is an explicit boundary where a domain model and its ubiquitous language (shared terms between devs and domain experts) stay consistent.

title: CAP Theorem
description: CAP is the shorthand for a constraint on distributed data stores: you cannot simultaneously promise that every read is up to date (consistency), that every request gets a response (availability), and that the system keeps working when th…

title: Domain Modeling
description: Domain modeling is how you represent business concepts and rules in code—orders, accounts, prescriptions—not as anonymous rows and DTOs, but as types the business already talks about.

title: Eventual Consistency
description: Eventual consistency means replicas may disagree for a while, but if writes stop, every copy converges to the same state.

title: Idempotency
description: An idempotent operation leaves the system in the same state whether you run it once or many times with the same intent.

title: PACELC Theorem
description: PACELC extends the CAP theorem.

title: Quality Attributes (Non-Functional Requirements)
description: Quality attributes (QAs), also called non-functional requirements (NFRs), describe how well a system performs its job — not what features it exposes.

title: Reference Architectures
description: A reference architecture (RA) is a validated blueprint for a recurring system shape — web portals, event pipelines, data planes — that teams adapt instead of debating every cross-cutting choice from zero.

title: Architectural Trade-off Analysis
description: Architectural trade-off analysis compares design candidates against weighted quality attributes so the team records what it gains and what it gives up.

title: API Governance – System Design Practices
description: API governance is the combination of standards, tooling, and lifecycle controls that keep an organization’s HTTP and event interfaces consistent, secure, and safe for consumers to depend on over time.

title: Architecture Governance – System Design Practices
description: Architecture governance is the set of processes, roles, and controls that steer how an organization defines, changes, and sustains its systems so they stay aligned with business goals and agreed quality attributes.

title: Architecture Review Process
